To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

intestinal stem cell activity in response to bacteria is a consequence of both oxidative burst and immune signaling, that the JAK/STAT and JNK pathways are required for stem cell proliferation in response to bacteria, and that the gut microbiota modulates stem cell activity at basal levels.

the intestinal stem cell activity is controlled by multiple pathways, which are both immune-dependent and immune-independent, and that this activity is crucial for the defense of the intestinal barrier.

the increased epithelial renewal observed in the Drosophilia intestine upon some bacterial infections, as well as in the absence of the immune system, is a consequence of oxidative burst and that it requires the JNK and JAK-STAT pathways.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the molecular mechanisms that govern the homeostasis of the Drosphila gut, and how it is affected by the microbiota.
the role of bacteria in the regulation of stem cell proliferation.
the study of intestinal homeostasis, a complex interplay between immune and developmental pathways, which is essential for the maintenance of the gut epithelium.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
gut homeostatic balance is achieved through a complex interplay between stem cell activity, gut microbiota and the immune system.
the intestinal stem cell activity is a key factor in the control of gut homeostasis and that its alteration may be at the origin of inflammatory disorders and/or cancerous lesions of this organ.
the microbiota and the innate immune system are both required to maintain intestinal homeostasis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
gut homeostatic control is a consequence of an interplay between the immune system, the gut microbiota and the intestinal stem cell activity.
the intestinal stem cells (ISCs) are a key component of the Drosophilas gut defense.
the microbiota is a key factor for intestinal stem cell activity and that this activity is required for intestinal immunity against bacterial infections.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the intestinal stem cells are an integral component of the gut immune system, and that their activity is regulated in response to both infectious and indigenous microbiota.
the intestinal stem cells are not just the cells that are renewing the epithelium, but that they are also the cells that are sensing and responding to the presence of the microbiota.
the intestinal stem cells are a major target of the immune response to gut microbiota.
